The economics of heat pump retrofits in old homes

Published 2026-10-06 19:30 UTC

Over the past three years our small energy consultancy has helped owners of 40 pre-war houses replace oil and gas boilers with heat pumps. The most important lesson is simple: insulate first, then size the heat pump to the improved house, not to the old boiler.

Many of the houses had boilers rated at 30 kilowatts or more, far larger than needed. After air sealing, attic insulation and new storm windows, the measured heat loss on a cold design day dropped by an average of 35 percent. Most homes ended up with heat pumps rated between 9 and 14 kilowatts.

Right-sizing matters because oversized heat pumps cycle on and off frequently, which reduces efficiency and comfort. Undersized units, on the other hand, rely on backup electric resistance heat during cold snaps, which raises bills. We used room-by-room heat loss calculations and checked them against past fuel bills to avoid both problems.

Costs varied widely. Insulation and air sealing averaged about $9,000 per house, and heat pump installation averaged $18,000 before incentives. Federal tax credits and state rebates covered roughly 40 percent of the total in most cases. Houses with existing radiators sometimes needed a few larger radiators in rooms that were hard to heat at lower water temperatures.

Running costs depended heavily on local electricity prices. In our region, households switching from oil saved an average of $1,100 a year, while those switching from natural gas saw costs roughly unchanged but gained air conditioning in summer. Payback periods ranged from 7 to 15 years.

The biggest surprises were older electrical panels that needed upgrades and the difficulty of finding installers experienced with hydronic systems. We have published our spreadsheet of house data and measurements for anyone planning similar retrofits.

Several readers have asked about cold climates. Our coldest homes saw design temperatures of minus 15 Celsius, and modern cold-climate units handled them without backup heat once the envelope work was done.
